title: How does culture shape the way mental health is understood in the Gulf?
citation: Mirzai, F., Nasiri, Z., Naeim, M., Imannezhad, S., & Javedani, M. (2024). Advancing mental health in the Middle East: a paradigm shift. Asian Journal of Psychiatry, 101, 104220.
content:
How does culture shape the way mental health is understood in the Gulf?

Culture influences how people understand emotional distress, when they seek support and who they turn to first. Across many Gulf Arab communities, family, religion, and community play an important role in everyday life and are often seen as the first sources of comfort during difficult times. Mental health is therefore often understood within these wider social and spiritual contexts rather than only through a medical or psychological lens. While awareness of mental health has grown significantly across the Gulf in recent years, attitudes and beliefs still vary between families, generation and individuals.

Doesn't seeking help mean something is wrong with my faith or family?

One common misconception is that needing psychological support means a person lacks faith, has failed to cope, or reflects badly on their family. In reality, emotional wellbeing and faith are not opposites. Many people draw strength from their religious beliefs while also benefiting from professional support. Seeking help does not mean abandoning personal values or family traditions. It is simply another way of caring for your health, much like seeking treatment for a physical illness.

Why is mental health still hard to talk about openly?

Mental health can be difficult to discuss because many Gulf societies place a strong value on privacy, family reputation, resilience and maintaining harmony within the family. People may worry about burdening loved ones, being misunderstood, or attracting unwanted attention from others. These concerns often lead people to keep their struggles private, even when they would benefit from support. As public awareness grows, these conversations are becoming more common, but change often happens gradually.

What does mental health stigma look like day to day?

Stigma is not always obvious or intentional. It may appear as avoiding conversations about emotions, encouraging someone to simply "stay strong," dismissing emotional distress as temporary weakness, or worrying about what others might think if someone seeks therapy. Some people hide their appointments or avoid telling family members they are receiving support because they fear being judged. These experiences can make it harder to reach out, even when someone knows that support could help.

Privacy and discretion vs stigma: what's the difference?

Wanting privacy is not the same as experiencing stigma. Many people, regardless of culture, prefer to keep personal matters within a small circle of trusted people and this is a healthy personal choice. Stigma is different because it involves fear of shame, judgement, or negative consequences simply for experiencing emotional difficulties or seeking help. Someone can value privacy while still believing that mental health deserves the same care and respect as physical health.

Why does my family see this differently than I do?

Differences in opinion about mental health are common, particularly between generations or family members with different life experiences. Older relatives may have grown up at a time when emotional difficulties were rarely discussed openly, while younger generations may have greater exposure to mental health education through schools, workplaces and social media. These differences do not necessarily mean one perspective is right or wrong. They often reflect changing social attitudes, personal experiences and different understandings of wellbeing.

How can I get support in a way that fits my values and family?

There is no single right way to seek support. Some people choose to speak with a trusted family member before seeing a therapist, while others prefer to keep therapy private until they feel comfortable sharing it. Many people also find that professional support can sit comfortably alongside their cultural values, religious beliefs and family relationships. The goal is not to replace these important sources of support, but to build on them in a way that respects what matters most to you.
